title: Yahweh Shut Him In — Enter, Shut, Rise
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. In the last lesson we saw the grief in God's heart, and we saw that in the very same passage he had already provided the ark. Noah built for something like a hundred years, and for something like a hundred years people laughed at him. In today's lesson, that ship is finally going to be used.

And the question this lesson asks may be exactly where you are living at the moment: have you ever been kept somewhere perfectly safe — and yet the door was shut by somebody else, and you could not get out? It might be a season of waiting. It might be an illness. It might be a responsibility you cannot walk away from, a position you want to leave and cannot leave.

Let me give you the answer up front: one and the same door, once it is shut, keeps the water out and keeps freedom out as well. And what decides whether the people inside are safe is not that door. It is the One who shut it.
1. "Come In" — the One Who Says It Is Already Inside
Verse 1: "Yahweh said to Noah, 'Come with all of your household into the ship.'"

There is a detail here that no translation carries across. The Hebrew is בֹּא־אַתָּה (*bo-atah*), literally "come in, you" — not "go in." Brothers and sisters, the one who says "come in" is standing inside.

Which is to say: God is not standing on the bank waving Noah aboard. God is inside the ark first, and from inside he says to Noah, come in. This is the same tone of voice as that sentence in chapter 3, "Where are you?" — God always arrives first, and then calls the person over.

Then God says, "for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation." Notice the order of that sentence against the previous chapter: 6:8 speaks first of finding favour, and only then does 6:9 call him a righteous man; and by 7:1 God confirms that righteousness with his own mouth. Grace comes first, being counted righteous comes second, and only then does this invitation come.

And there is another detail in verse 2 that often gets read straight past: "You shall take seven pairs of every clean animal with you, the male and his female." Brothers and sisters, Leviticus has not been written yet, Moses has not been born yet — so how did Noah know which animals were clean? The text does not explain. But at the very least this tells us something: God's mind was already being passed on before there was any written law. And those extra clean animals are exactly what gets used for the burnt offerings in 8:20 — if he had taken only a single pair, one offering would have wiped the species out. God had already worked out in advance even the sacrifice Noah would offer after he came off the boat.
God says "come in" rather than "go in" — is that difference really so important?

Yes. The Hebrew of 7:1 is בֹּא (*bo*), "come", not "go." The one who says "come" is himself inside. That single word tells us that the ark did not hold only eight people and a great many animals — God was already there. And this settles the shape of the whole of salvation: it is not God standing outside pushing us in; it is God going in first and then calling us to come. Which is why the Lord Jesus in the Gospels also says "come to me", and not "go over there." For a frightened person the difference is very practical: you are not being thrown into somewhere unknown. You are being called in to a God who is already inside.
2. Seven Days, Forty Days, a Hundred and Fifty Days
Verse 4: "In seven days, I will cause it to rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights."

"In seven days" — עוֹד שִׁבְעָה (*od shiv'ah*). Brothers and sisters, those seven days were not easy. The ship was finished. The animals were aboard. And not one drop of rain had yet fallen out of the sky. The neighbours were probably still laughing. And through those seven days Noah had to go on believing, one day at a time, in something that had not happened.

In pastoral work I meet this situation constantly: God has spoken, and you have done what he said, and the thing still has not happened. Those seven days are the hardest stretch faith ever walks — not the most dangerous stretch, the most embarrassing one.

Then comes "forty days and forty nights." Brothers and sisters, this is the first time the number forty appears in the Bible. Later Moses will be on the mountain forty days and forty nights, Elijah will walk forty days and forty nights to Horeb, and the Lord Jesus will be forty days and forty nights in the wilderness under temptation. From here on, forty in Scripture is almost always fastened to a stretch of days in which somebody is being shaped, tested, made new.

Verse 11 says, "all the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the sky's windows opened." Look at the voice of those two verbs. "Burst open" is נִבְקְעוּ (*nivqe'u*), a passive — the deep did not split itself open; it was split open. Brothers and sisters, in chapter 1 God divided the waters above from the waters below and made the dry land appear; here both of those partitions are pulled down together. The world falls back into chaos.

So the flood is not an unusually large rainstorm. It is creation being undone. That matters, because it explains why salvation could never be a matter of improvement — the world was broken to the point where it had to be begun again. And that wind blowing over the face of the water in 8:1 uses exactly the word 1:2 used.
Was the flood global or local? Does the pulpit have to settle it?

This is a long-standing dispute in interpretation, and there are mainly two readings. The first is a global flood, taking 7:19 — "All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered" — at face value. The second is a flood that was local but covered the whole of the world as it was then known, on the grounds that the Hebrew word for "earth" (אֶרֶץ) often means one particular region, and that "under the whole sky" can equally mean the extent of what people then knew. Godly interpreters hold both readings, and neither of them touches the truth of salvation. What these notes do is set both out, decline to rule, and add a reminder: the point of this chapter is not how high the water rose. It is what God said, who went in, and who shut the door. Preach a disputed question as though it were the test of somebody's faith, and you will push people away.
Seven days, forty days, a hundred and fifty days — do these numbers mean anything?

The text itself does not explain them, but these numbers do come round again and again in Scripture: seven is completeness; forty is repeatedly tied to testing and preparation (forty years in the wilderness, the Lord Jesus fasting forty days); and a hundred and fifty days is about five months, the long stretch in which the waters went "on and on." What we have to be careful of is turning them into a code and calculating dates with them — and that is one of the iron rules of this whole course. The safer reading is to look at what each one does. The seven days are a cushion of grace, leaving room for one more person to come aboard. The forty days are how long the judgement lasts. The hundred and fifty days are the length of the waiting. And waiting is often more wearing than the disaster itself — which, for anyone in a long hard season today, is a real comfort.
3. A Light from the Original: Who Shut That Door
Verse 16, the heart of the whole chapter: "Those who went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God commanded him; then Yahweh shut him in."
I want you to read that last line once more, slowly: then Yahweh shut him in.

The word "shut" is וַיִּסְגֹּר (*vayisgor*) — to close a door, to seal it up. And the subject of that verb is Yahweh. Brothers and sisters, this verse does not say Noah shut the door, and it does not say the family put their shoulders to it together. God shut it.
And that one small detail settles two very large problems at a stroke.

The first problem is safety. Outside, forty days and forty nights of rain; the waters rose and lifted the whole ship. If Noah had shut that door himself, then every time the hull lurched he would have thought: is the door working loose? Did I bolt it properly just now? But God shut the door. So the people inside did not have to guard the door. They only had to stay alive.

The second problem is freedom. If God shut the door, that also means they could not open it. For more than a year — eight people, countless living creatures, an ocean on every side — with no way out. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the question I asked at the very beginning: when you are shut inside a place, who shut the door?
If the enemy shut it, that is a prison. If you shut it yourself by making a mess of things, that is a consequence. But if God shut it — then that same enclosed space has a name, and the name is ark.

And notice this: in the whole chapter, not once does the text record a single thing Noah said inside. No prayer. No complaint. Not one line of dialogue. The text records only this: he went in, the door was shut, the water rose. Some seasons of life are exactly like that. There is no story to tell. There is only the waiting.
"Then Yahweh shut him in" — why does that one sentence matter so much?

Because if a person shuts the door, that person will go on wanting to open it. You would hear the knocking outside, the crying outside, and your own hand would be resting on the bolt. God shutting the door himself takes the whole weight of "should I open it?" off Noah's shoulders. The sentence says two things at once. First, the hour of judgement is set by God and not by people. Second, the responsibility for protection rests on God and not on the strength of your will. John 10 says, "I am the door", and the same chapter says, "No one is able to snatch them out of my Father's hand" — the same kind of safety. And for us it is very practical: the reason you are still standing today is not that you are gripping tightly enough. It is that Someone shut the door for you.
Once the door was shut, was there no chance left for the people outside? Isn't God being too severe?

Look first at the timescale: the ship took a hundred years to build, and 2 Peter calls Noah "a preacher of righteousness" — which is to say that all through that century a warning was being given. God's judgement is never a sudden turning of the face. As for what happened after the door was shut, Scripture has not given us a list of names, and we should not issue one on God's behalf. 1 Peter 3:19–20 says that Christ "went and preached to the spirits in prison", and that verse itself carries several interpretations; it is not a place to build doctrine. The healthy posture is this: preach God's mercy fully, preach the reality of judgement fully, and then put your strength into the door that is still open — because today the door is still open, and that is the part we can actually do.
4. The Waters Rose Very High, and Not One Line Is Sensationalised
Verses 17 to 24 are the heaviest stretch in the chapter: "The waters rose very high on the earth. All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered."

Brothers and sisters, I want you to notice how the author writes. This is the largest disaster in human history, and there is not one sentence of dramatisation in the account. No description of screaming. No description of struggling. Not a single close-up. It simply records, one line at a time: the waters rose, the mountains were covered, everything on the earth with flesh in it died.

That restraint is itself a posture. The author does not want you gawping at a spectacle, and he does not want you excited by other people's destruction. He wants you to know one thing: the judgement is real.

And in the middle of that same passage, at the end of verse 23, one line is slipped in: "Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship." Brothers and sisters, this is how the Bible always writes — in the blackest paragraph there is always a sentence that says "only there was left." Isaiah, Jeremiah, all the way down to Romans 11: what they are talking about is this same remnant.

And then verse 24: "The waters flooded the earth one hundred fifty days." A hundred and fifty days. Five months. After the forty days of rain had stopped, there were still a hundred and ten days in which nothing whatever happened. The door was still shut, the water was still up, the ship was still drifting.

Brothers and sisters, a great many people assume that the hardest part of faith is the storm. Very often it is not. The hardest part is the stretch after the rain stops, when nothing at all is happening.
The text writes about the waters rising and never once plays it up. What is that way of writing meant to teach us?

The Bible is at its most restrained exactly where its material is most horrifying. Chapter 7 records no screaming, no bodies, no close-up shots — only the water rising, the mountains covered, the breath cut off. That way of writing carries two things. The first is respect: death is not raw material for dramatic effect. The second is emphasis: what the text wants you to attend to is that God's word came true, not how spectacular a disaster can be. And this is very useful to us today. When you preach about a disaster, about an epidemic, about a war, do not work people's emotions up with pictures. Godliness whipped up that way usually does not survive a week, and it leaves people numb to suffering. Learn the Bible's way of writing: tell the truth, and add nothing to it.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is turning the pulpit into a debating floor for geology. Global flood or regional flood — the dispute is real, godly scholars genuinely do differ, and we handle it separately on the map of disputed questions. But the point of chapter 7 is God's judgement and God's keeping. If you spend a whole sermon arguing about rock strata, your congregation will go home having learned a position, and they will not have heard that door close.

The second is preaching only how terrible the judgement is and never preaching the invitation to come in. Look at the order: God says first, "Come with all of your household into the ship", and only seven days later does the rain fall. The door opens first; the water comes afterwards. Preach the water without the door and what the congregation hears is a threat, not the gospel. The last picture in this sermon ought to be an open door, not water closing over people's heads.

The third is turning "a household of eight" into "believe, and your whole family is guaranteed to be saved." Noah's family went into the ark with him, and that was grace — not a formula that takes effect automatically. Acts 16:31 says, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household"; that is a promise, and it is an invitation, but it does not cancel each person's own response. Preach it as a guarantee and the brothers and sisters whose families have not yet believed will be trapped in endless self-blame.

The fourth is treating "being shut in" as simply the same thing as God punishing you. The door in verse 16 is protection, not penalty. One and the same set of circumstances can be a cell or an ark, and the difference lies in who shut it and why. If that is not carefully distinguished, your congregation will begin reading every difficulty in their lives as a beating from God — and that will crush them.

The fifth is preaching Noah as a hero who sailed through it all serenely. The text does not tell us how he felt in there, and we should not pile serenity onto him on his behalf. More than a year shut inside a boat full of animals is not a cruise. Admit that those days were hard, and your congregation will believe that you understand their hard days too.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: I have prayed for my family's salvation for years and nothing has moved — is it because I am not good enough? Brothers and sisters, this one has to be answered very carefully. First: Noah's whole household went into the ark, and that was grace, and it is worth asking God for exactly that for our own families. Second: the text records the other side of it at the same time — in those hundred and twenty years, apart from his own household, not one outsider came aboard, and 2 Peter 2:5 still calls him "Noah, a preacher of righteousness." He spoke; nobody listened. So please hold two things apart: your faithfulness, and other people's response. You may keep building the ship and keep preaching — that is your responsibility. Whether somebody else comes aboard is a matter between him and God. If you post other people's decisions to the account of your own spiritual life, you will be crushed, and that weight was never laid on you by God.

The second question: Chinese people are very afraid of "bad luck" and of having "offended something", so when something goes wrong the instinct is to hunt for a cause, to find out what was offended. When a Christian meets a disaster, how should he think? I would suggest holding two lines. The first line: do not read every disaster as somebody's sin. In John 9:3 the disciples ask, about the man born blind, who it was that sinned, and the Lord Jesus says straight out, "This man didn't sin, nor did his parents"; in Luke 13:4 the Lord Jesus brings up the eighteen who were killed when the tower in Siloam fell, and he says plainly that they were no worse offenders than anybody else. The second line: a disaster really is a warning, and the Lord Jesus' own conclusion in that same passage is, "unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way." So the right response is not to go looking for who offended what. It is to turn round and look at your own heart. The first makes people afraid; the second brings people home.
My family does not believe. How do I "call them to come" instead of pushing at them all the time?

Start by changing one habit: most of the time we are telling, and very seldom inviting. "Come in" is an invitation, and an invitation has three parts — I am inside, it is good here, and I want you here too. So in practice: first, let them see whether the way you are inside is actually better; that is more powerful than any argument. Second, replace the sentences that judge with sentences that invite — "this Sunday I'd like to take you somewhere" works far better than "if you don't believe soon it will be too late." Third, accept being turned down, and then go on loving without changing your manner. Noah built that ship for a hundred years; we too should be prepared for a long wait.
7. Living 321 Out — Hand the Door Over to God
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Noah goes in, and then God shuts the door. And in John 10:9 the Lord Jesus says, "I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out and will find pasture." Brothers and sisters, that verse takes the picture in this chapter to its summit: God does not only shut the door; he himself becomes the door. The door of the ark was made of wood. Our door is a Lord who died for us.

The Bible is my standard — three times in this chapter, at verses 5, 9 and 16, the phrase "as God commanded" appears. Three times. The author is confirming one and the same thing: Noah changed nothing. And verse 5, "Noah did everything that Yahweh commanded him", is the same Hebrew sentence as 6:22, "He did all that God commanded him" — word for word, with only the name of God changing. That is what a standard means: the same verdict can be written over your life a second time.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — guidance is sometimes a matter of moving forward, and sometimes a matter of being told to go in and then stay there. The guidance in chapter 7 is the second kind. Brothers and sisters, we are very used to imagining that being led by the Spirit means a new direction, a new opportunity, a new door opening. But there is a kind of guidance that says: go in, sit down, wait. That is guidance every bit as much as the other.

Let Jesus be King — the handle is not on the inside of that door. The hardest lesson in letting Jesus be King is accepting that this particular matter is not mine to decide. That is not resignation; it is handing sovereignty back to the Lord who has the power to shut and the power to open. Revelation 3:7 says of him that he "opens and no one can shut, and who shuts and no one opens."

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice how much the human beings actually do in this chapter: they go in. That is all. Every other verb has God as its subject: God commands, God sends the rain, God shuts the door, God raises the waters, God makes the waters go down. The people who were saved contributed almost no effort to the whole process. That is what grace looks like.

Establish God's system — the ark did not hold only eight people; it held every kind of living creature. What was inside was a whole world, preserved intact. Brothers and sisters, what God preserved was not a hero. It was a system. So to establish God's system is to prepare a place capable of carrying the next generation — your home and your small group are both part of that ship.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put a great deal of weight on action, on practice, on getting things implemented, and that is right, because faith without works is dead. But chapter 7 reminds us that there is a kind of obedience whose content is doing nothing at all. For the year and more after that door closed, the only thing Noah could do was stay inside. If we define the spiritual life purely as constantly doing something, then in a season of waiting brothers and sisters will conclude that they are going backwards. In fact they may be standing in the most obedient position of their lives.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Shut Door
Brothers and sisters, one and the same door lands in four kinds of heart, and in each of them it feels entirely different.

The proud heart says: "I am on the boat, and they are in the water." When this heart finishes chapter 7, what it feels most strongly is separateness, and safety, and even a small flicker of satisfaction. Brothers and sisters, notice the restraint of the text — it does not hand you a single line you could gloat over. And Ezekiel 33:11 says, "'As I live,' says the Lord Yahweh, 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live.'" If God himself takes no pleasure in it, what gives us the right?

The fearful heart says: "What if I am the one shut outside?" The moment this heart reads about judgement it begins auditing itself to see whether it qualifies. To a heart like that I want to say: look at who shut the door. Your salvation does not rest on how tightly you hold on; it rests on how firmly he shut it. John 10:28 says, "They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand."

The ashamed heart says: "Someone like me probably only deserves to stand outside the door." Brothers and sisters, look at what God says in verse 1: "Come with all of your household into the ship." That is an invitation, not a selection process. And the One who issued the invitation is already inside, waiting.

The wounded heart says: "Then what about this shut door I am living behind right now?" You may be inside a situation with no way out of it — an illness, caring for a family member, a marriage at a deadlock, a wait with no end in sight. Brothers and sisters, I am not going to tell you glibly, "this must be an ark." All I can tell you is the clue this chapter gives: the door was shut by God, and he has not forgotten you — the very first sentence of the next chapter is "God remembered Noah." You are still in chapter 7. But chapter 8 will come.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, write down what the shut door in your life is at present. Write it honestly; it does not have to sound spiritual. When you have written it, add a prayer beside it: "Lord, if this door was shut by you, settle me down inside it; and if it was not, let me see that clearly."

Second, practise once this week the obedience of not doing. Find one matter you keep wanting to reach into and which is in fact not yours to reach into, and deliberately do nothing. Take that time and pray instead. This is harder than doing one more thing.

Third, pray by name for seven days for one family member who is "not yet aboard" — and at the same time hand the outcome over. At the end of every one of those prayers add this line: "Lord, his response is a matter between him and you. My part is only to go on loving him."

Fourth, look back on a season when you were once shut in, and write down three things God did during those days. Once you have them written down, you will find it easier to trust him for the season you are in now.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences: the Bible records a great flood, but what moves me most is not the water — it is one very small line, "then Yahweh shut him in"; he did not shut that door himself, so however hard the storm outside, he never had to guard the door; and the Bible later says that door has a name, because he said, "I am the door."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I am not in charge of that door, and that I do not need to be; all I need to do is go into the place he named.
I declare that in the days of waiting, doing nothing at all can be the deepest obedience of all.
I declare that I will go on building the ship that is in my hands, and will not measure my faithfulness by other people's response.
I declare that the One who shuts the door is also the One who opens it — what he shuts no one can open, and what he opens no one can shut.
This week I am supposed to "go in through that door", but I feel I am not qualified to go in. What do I do?

Look at who that sentence was spoken to: "Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation." The words "I have seen your righteousness" are God's words; they are not Noah's assessment of himself. Genesis 6:8 said it earlier still: "But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes" — favour first, and only then being counted righteous. So the qualification is not something you carry in with you; it is given by the God who spoke. In practice: if there is a sentence inside you that keeps saying "I am not worthy", write it down, write that verse beside it, and read the verse out loud. The feeling will not change straight away, but you will know that your feeling is not the final judge.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, I want it to be the last five words of verse 16: "then Yahweh shut him in."

Picture it for a moment. The door closes. Inside, everything suddenly goes quiet — nothing left but the noises of the animals and the working of the timber. Outside, it begins to rain. And those eight people stand there, able to do nothing at all.

And through the year and more that followed, every time the hull lurched, every time the water slammed against the planking, there was one thing they could be sure of — we are not the ones who shut this door.

Brothers and sisters, this is the comfort this chapter has for you. If you are in a stretch of days with no way out, the question to ask is not "when do I get out?" but "who shut this door?" And if he shut it, then before you come out, nothing whatever can get in.

And 1 Peter 3:20–21 says of those eight souls that they "were saved through water", and says that the baptism this water pictures "now saves you … through the resurrection of Jesus Christ." The same flood: to the people outside it was destruction, and to the people inside it was rescue. What decided the difference was not how deep the water was. It was which side of the door you were on.

The focus is not on how hard this stretch of days has been for me, not on when I get to come out, and not on whether other people come aboard. The focus is on Jesus — he himself is the door, and he himself is the one who shut me inside. No longer I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us to settle down this week behind that shut door, because the One who shut it is remembering us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear conviction.
1. ★★★ What God said was "come in", not "go in." What shape does that one word give to salvation?
2. ★★ "Then Yahweh shut him in" — if Noah had shut that door himself, what would have been different about the forty days that followed?
3. ★ The text writes the flood with no dramatisation at all. What does that way of writing warn us about when we talk about disasters and bad news?
4. ★★ A hundred years of building, and not one extra person came aboard. What does that say to the idea that only results count as success?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can hold this door myself), fearful (the water outside keeps rising), ashamed (I am not worthy to go in), wounded (somebody once shut a door in my face). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Come with all of your household into the ship." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something in you right now that you have been holding shut by willpower, and holding until you are worn out? If you let God be the one who shuts that door, what would be different?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The family member I most want to bring in through this door is …"
9. ★★ This week, what kind of invitation are you going to make to that person? Say out loud the actual sentence you will use.

Leader's reminder: questions five and nine will touch the helplessness of having family who do not believe. If someone has been trying for years and has still seen no result, affirm his perseverance first; do not bombard him with methods, and never say to him, "your faith isn't strong enough."
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ "I am inside, it is good here, and I want you here too" — in your own home, how will you let people see that the first of those three is true?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, does the way you live make anybody want to ask, "why are you different from everyone else?"
12. ★★★ The hundred-year practice: this week, pray for that family member on a fixed schedule for seven days — once a day, one minute each time. Say which slot in the day you will do it in.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the name of that family member, and ask him to pray along with you. Say both names out loud now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, what God said to Noah was "come in", not "go in." Second, that means he had already gone in ahead. Third, so the God I believe in is not outside the door hurrying me along; he is inside the door waiting for me. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the person you are going to invite this week, and who you are going to tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord himself to shut for us the doors we have been holding shut until we are worn out.
